newsitem.title: MALI: Mali shuts schools in poll run-up, warns opponents.
newsitem.headline: Mali shuts schools in poll run-up, warns opponents.

text.p: Mali ordered schools to close on Wednesday and said student demonstrations had been planned with opposition politicians to sow disorder in the run-up to a Sunday presidential election.

"There was a meeting between students and opposition leaders. They adopted a scenario to create a situation ripe for insurrection during which blood would flow," government spokesman Bakare Konimba Traore said in a televised statement.
Security forces on Monday fired teargas to clear students who threw stones and burned campaign posters of President Alpha Oumar Konare, who stands for reelection on Sunday in a contentious election.

The multi-party presidential poll is the impoverished West African country's second since independence from France in 1960 and seen as a key test of democracy, but opposition parties have called for a boycott.

The students, who are protesting against a slow and chaotic start to the school year, also want the departure of Konare -- whose insistence on keeping a May 11 date for the presidential poll outraged opposition supporters.

"The government will prevent anyone who wants to come to power by other means than the ballot box," Traore said. He added that schools and colleges would be shut until Tuesday to ensure that children did not get hurt.

Political analysts in Bamako compare the current wave of student demonstrations, power and water strikes with the tension which gripped the city before the 1991 overthrow of former one-party ruler General Moussa Traore by the military.
Widespread praise greeted Mali's 1992 transition from single-party dictatorship to multi-party democracy.

But serious organisational problems disrupted parliamentary elections in April, during which Malians turned out in force only to be frustrated by lack of ballot papers and problems with voter cards and lists.
The constitutional court in the former French colony scrapped the results citing irregularities although a date for a new ballot has not yet been set.

In the wake of the April 13 election confusion opposition parties called on the constitutional court to scrap the decree allowing Sunday's vote to go ahead. Konare, who has delayed the elections by a week, says they must go ahead this time.
The court has yet to rule on the opposition's appeal.
Konare, a historian elected in 1992, has steered the country on a course of economic liberalisation. He has won praise from the World Bank and the United States for his efforts.
His only challenger is businessman Hamadou Maribatrou Diaby.
